body: For a frequency band defined by lower and upper bounds [f_low, f_high) and a spectral decomposition with N frequency bins indexed i=1..N, each with a complex amplitude A_i and frequency f_i where f_low <= f_i < f_high: the distribution is the ordered vector v = (|A_1|^2, |A_2|^2, ..., |A_N|^2), where |A_i|^2 is the energy of bin i. The parameters are the band bounds and the spectral decomposition method. The persistence mechanism is the explicit storage of the N-tuple of non-negative scalars ordered by bin index. [formal: the mathematical representation | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral sequence is an ordered array of cepstral coefficients indexed by coefficient position, representing signal characteristics in the cepstral domain. Parameters: (1) number of coefficients N (typically 12-20 for speech), (2) coefficient type — filterbank-based MFCC, DFT-based, or DCT-based cepstral coefficients, (3) normalization method — mean-normalized, variance-normalized, or raw. The persistence mechanism maps (coefficient type, count, normalization) to a fixed-length vector c[1..N] where each element c[i] represents the i-th cepstral coefficient. [formal: cepstrum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Jitter (period perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the cycle-to-cycle variation of the fundamental period in a voiced speech signal. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, the perturbation is computed as APQ1 = (1/(N-1)) * Σ_i |P_{i+1} - P_i| / ((1/N) * Σ_i P_i), or equivalently the standard deviation of the periods divided by their mean, reported in percent or in absolute units (milliseconds or seconds). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle period measure, (3) the perturbation variant (APQ1 — average absolute difference, JRR — ratio, JDP — absolute difference). Small jitter indicates period stability (normal phonation); large jitter indicates period instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. [formal: titubatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A spectral moment is a quantitative descriptor obtained by weighting each frequency bin of a spectral energy distribution by a power of its center frequency and summing across all bins. The n-th spectral moment is mu_n = sum_i (f_i^n * E_i) where f_i is the center frequency of bin i and E_i is the spectral energy in that bin. The zeroth moment yields total spectral energy; the first moment yields the energy-weighted mean frequency; the second central moment yields variance; higher moments characterize asymmetry (skewness) and tail heaviness (kurtosis). The construct persists as a parameterized computational routine implementable in software or hardware, standardized across audio analysis toolkits and music information retrieval systems. [formal: spectral_moment | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A Kaiser window is a parameterized family of window functions defined by the zeroth-order modified Bessel function. Its formula is: w(n) = I₀(πβ√(1−((2n−(N−1))/(N))²)) / I₀(πβ) for 0 ≤ n ≤ N−1, where I₀ is the zeroth-order modified Bessel function of the first kind, N is the window length, and β is the shape parameter. The β parameter controls the tradeoff between main-lobe width and side-lobe attenuation: β = 0 yields a rectangular window; β = 2.43 is optimal for DFT analysis; β = 3.44 approximates a Hamming window; β = 5 gives ≈−43 dB side lobes; β = 6 gives ≈−47 dB; β ≥ 9 approaches the Blackman-Harris form. The family is designed to achieve the maximum main-lobe concentration for a given side-lobe level — optimal for a specified side-lobe constraint. Persistence mechanism: the Bessel-function formula codified in DSP literature and implemented in all major signal-processing toolkits. [formal: fenestra kaißer | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.5]

Spectral-band-smoothness is a spectral analysis measure that quantifies how smoothly the per-bin energy values change across frequency within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum. It computes a weighted mean absolute derivative of adjacent bin energies, normalized by the sub-band's mean energy and the number of bins, yielding a dimensionless index of spectral continuity. Parameters: the frequency sub-band bounds (f_min, f_max), the FFT bin energy vector, and optionally a window function for the energy estimation. The persistence mechanism is the algorithmic computation over the sub-band's energy profile. [formal: smoothness | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.30]

For a frequency band with N energy bins having energies E_1, E_2, ..., E_N: the RMS energy is the square root of the mean of squared energies. The parameter is the frequency band definition (lower and upper bounds). The persistence mechanism is RMS = sqrt((1/N) * sum(E_i^2)) over N bins within the band. Display trailer: [formal: rms energy | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

For a spectral decomposition with N frequency bins indexed i=1..N, each with center frequency f_i and complex amplitude A_i, the per-bin energy vector is the ordered tuple v = (|A_1|², |A_2|², …, |A_N|²) of non-negative scalars ordered by bin index, each entry being the energy of its bin. It is parameterized by the decomposition and a bin range [i_min, i_max] within 1..N: at the full range the vector covers all bins of the spectrum; at a range covering exactly the bins whose centers fall in a frequency band [f_low, f_high) it is the band-restricted vector. Persistence mechanism: explicit storage of the ordered tuple as the substrate operand that spectral descriptors read their per-bin energies, means, centroids, and maxima from directly, rather than from any scalar summary. [formal: vector energiae binarum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-onset detects the emergence of new frequency content by measuring the increase in spectral energy between consecutive time frames. Given consecutive power spectra P[k,t] and P[k,t-1], the spectral onset function O[t] = max(P[k,t] - P[k,t-1], 0) summed across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) the power spectrum P[k,t] as the input domain, (2) the frame rate and windowing scheme, (3) the frequency band of interest. The persistence mechanism is the frame-to-frame difference of the power spectrum, thresholded by a half-wave rectifier, which distinguishes onset frames from sustained or decaying content. [formal: spectralis initium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-subband partitions the frequency axis into a contiguous range [f_lower, f_upper] within the overall spectrum. Given a sampling rate F_s and N frequency bins indexed by k = 0..N-1, a subband is defined by index range [k_1, k_2] where f_lower = k_1·F_s/N and f_upper = (k_2+1)·F_s/N. Parameters: (1) the spectral resolution (bin width F_s/N), (2) the frequency range [f_lower, f_upper] defining the subband, (3) the spectral representation (power spectrum, magnitude spectrum, or coefficients) over which the subband operates. The persistence mechanism is the contiguous index range [k_1, k_2] over the frequency axis, which enables independent processing of frequency content within the band. [formal: spectralis subbanda | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Text-linguistics is a human-made discipline of linguistics — the study of the structure, coherence, and function of extended texts (discourses) as structured wholes that extend beyond the sentence level. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the unit of analysis is the text or discourse as an integrated semantic-pragmatic entity, governed by relations of cohesion (grammatical and lexical ties across clauses), coherence (understandable logical and semantic connections), and communicative purpose (the function the text serves in interaction); (2) the analytical tools include discourse structure analysis (narrative, argumentative, expository patterns), information structure (theme-rheme, given-new), referential continuity (pronoun chains, anaphora resolution), and textual genre conventions that organize texts for specific communicative situations. Text-linguistics persists as a discipline that produces descriptions of textual organization across languages, models of discourse interpretation, and applications in text technology, rhetoric, discourse analysis, and language pedagogy. Paradigmatic cases: Halliday and Hasan's cohesion analysis, van Dijk's discourse semantics, rhetorical structure theory. [formal: textus-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral-median (median frequency) is the full-spectrum energy-quantile summary that reports the frequency f_med at which half of the total spectral energy lies below and half above. Parameters: (1) the per-bin energy vector E = {E_i} over the full analyzed spectrum [f0, f_max), (2) the energy-weighted cumulative distribution C(f) = (sum of E_i for bins at frequency <= f) / (sum of all E_i), (3) the target quantile q, which the median fixes at q = 0.5; the reported value is the smallest frequency f such that C(f) >= q. It is a member of the same quantile family as spectral-rolloff, which fixes q at the 85% energy level: the median is the 50% level of that family and does not depend on a chosen high-level contour. It reads the full per-bin energy vector and carries no [f_low, f_high) band bounds, so it is a full-side summary rather than a band-local one. Persists as a standard energy-quantile summary in audio analysis, computed on the per-bin energy vector in MIR toolkits and reported in sound-description documentation. [formal: mediana spectri | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-crossover is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the median energy location of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band: the frequency at which the cumulative energy reaches 50 percent of the spectrum's total energy. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N with center frequencies f_i, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |A_i|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. Computed by ordering the bins in ascending frequency, accumulating the per-bin energies until the running total first reaches half of the total energy sum, and taking the center frequency of the bin at that crossing. The value is in hertz: a low crossover means most energy sits below the median frequency (dark spectrum), a high crossover means energy is pushed toward the upper bins (bright spectrum). It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-crossover, which restricts the same cumulative test to bins within [f_low, f_high). It differs from spectral-centroid (energy-weighted mean, sensitive to high-energy outliers) and from spectral-rolloff (the cumulative crossing at an arbitrary threshold such as 85 percent, measuring brightness rather than the median). Being the 50th percentile of the energy distribution, the crossover is robust to heavy-tailed energy. Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of the full-spectrum energy median in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits and MIR feature pipelines. [formal: medium spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-concentration is a spectral analysis measure quantifying how much of a spectrum's total energy is concentrated in a single specified bin, normalized by the spectrum's total energy. Given a spectrum with N bins having energies E_1, E_2, ..., E_N, the concentration at bin j is C_j = E_j / Σ_i E_i. The value ranges from 0 (energy spread across all bins) to approaching 1 (nearly all energy in one bin). Parameters: (1) the spectral estimate (periodogram, Welch's method, or spectrogram slice), (2) the per-bin energy vector across all frequency bins, (3) the target bin index j. Persistence mechanism: standardized definition of normalized per-bin energy share, used in audio analysis, speech processing, and music information retrieval as a level-invariant spectral descriptor. [formal: concentratio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The vocal-tract model is a human-made model of the vocal tract as an acoustic filter cavity in speech production, describing how the shape of the vocal tract resonates to shape the glottal source into speech sounds. Parameters: area function along tract length, formant frequencies and bandwidths, articulatory positions. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized as acoustic tube theory, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in phonetics; it persists as a reusable filter component of the source-filter framework. [formal: vocal-tract | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

The attack-time is a non-negative real-valued duration representing the time elapsed from the onset of a sound to the peak of its amplitude envelope. Parameters: (1) the amplitude envelope function of the sound, (2) the detected onset point (zero-crossing of the envelope derivative), (3) the peak point (global maximum of the envelope within the attack phase). The persistence mechanism identifies the onset as the first zero-crossing of the envelope's first derivative after silence, and the peak as the local maximum of the envelope following that onset, then computes the time difference. [formal: attack-time | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

Spectral increase is a metric capturing the temporal rise of spectral energy between consecutive analysis frames. Computed as the difference between the current frame's total spectral energy and the preceding frame's energy, normalized by the preceding frame's energy. Positive values indicate energy growth; negative values indicate decay. [formal: augmentatio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

spectral-band-peak(f_low, f_high) = max{E[i]} for all bins i where f_low <= f_center[i] < f_high. Parameters: f_low (Hz, lower band boundary), f_high (Hz, upper band boundary), sampling_rate (Hz, determines bin center frequencies), n_fft (int, FFT window size). Persistence: pointwise maximum of the power spectral density within the band. [formal: spectral-band-peak | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The energy-envelope is the per-frame time series of a signal's energy, a human-made representation derived from a discrete-time waveform by framing, windowing, and magnitude squaring. Parameters: (1) the analysis frame length (typically 20-40 ms), (2) the hop between successive frames, (3) the window function applied within each frame (e.g. Hamming, Hanning), and (4) the squaring convention - raw x^2(t), windowed |w(t) x(t)|^2, or the per-frame sum that projects to short-time-energy as its scalar value. Distinction: it is the energy series, not the per-frame scalar (short-time-energy) and not the per-sample Hilbert amplitude (amplitude-envelope); it is the operand on which temporal-centroid (first moment of the energy envelope) and onset-related energy readings operate. Persistence mechanism: standardized windowed computation across audio analysis and speech toolkits (librosa, Essentia, HTK, Praat), encoded in published feature-extraction pipelines. [formal: envelopium energiae | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The spectral-power-distribution is a non-negative real-valued function over a discrete frequency domain representing how signal power is distributed across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) the input signal, (2) the number of frequency bins N, (3) the sampling rate or frequency resolution. Computation: take the magnitude spectrum |X[k]| of the input signal, compute P[k] = |X[k]|² / N for each bin k, yielding a discrete distribution over frequencies. The values P[k] are non-negative and sum to the total signal power, forming a power distribution across the frequency axis. [formal: CONCEPT | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-variance is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum at a given analysis frame. It is the band-localized (second-moment) statistic of the spectral-band moment family, computed from the per-bin energy values inside the band. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high, e.g. ISO 266 third-octave band edges or analyst-specified limits), (2) the per-bin energy array E_i = |X[k]|^2 indexed by the frequency bins whose centers fall within [f_low, f_high). Computation: the within-band mean mu = (1/N) SUM E_i, then the within-band variance sigma^2 = (1/N) SUM (E_i - mu)^2; the result is a single scalar per frame, typically in normalized relative units or joules squared. It measures how spread out the energy is across the band's bins: a concentrated band (one dominant bin) has low band-variance, an evenly spread band has high. Persistence: recomputed from the input spectrum and the band boundaries at any point in an audio analysis pipeline; it is the second-moment counterpart of spectral-band-centroid (first moment) and the even-order companion to spectral-band-skewness (third) and spectral-band-kurtosis (fourth). Display: {variance, low_hz, high_hz, bins, mean_energy}. [formal: varietas spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The onset-envelope is a non-negative real-valued function of time representing the temporal strength of acoustic onsets in an audio signal. Parameters: (1) the input audio signal, (2) the analysis frame rate (samples per second or frames per second), (3) the onset detection function (e.g., spectral flux, energy difference, phase deviation) used to compute raw onset strength, (4) optional smoothing window length for post-processing. Computation: compute the onset detection function frame-by-frame, apply median or exponential smoothing to suppress spurious detections, optionally normalize to [0, 1]. The construct persists as a per-sample or per-frame vector synchronized with the input signal. Display: waveform or scalar trace aligned with audio time. [formal: envelopeum inceptionis | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-evenness is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying how uniformly energy is distributed across the frequency bins within a defined frequency sub-band, normalized by the band's mean energy. It is the coefficient of variation of the per-bin energy values: given a band with N bins having energies E_i for i=1..N, the evenness is σ/μ where μ = (1/N)·ΣE_i is the mean energy and σ = √((1/N)·Σ(E_i - μ)²) is the standard deviation of energies. The value is a dimensionless ratio: 0 when all bins carry identical energy (perfectly even), increasing without upper bound as energy becomes more concentrated in fewer bins. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high), (2) the per-bin energy vector E_i within those bounds. Persistence mechanism: standardized definition of energy dispersion normalized by mean, used in music information retrieval and audio classification as a level-invariant spectral descriptor. [formal: aequabilitas spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The reduction of spectral energy from its peak value across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) discrete power spectrum P[k] for k = 0, ..., N-1 where N is the number of frequency bins, (2) the maximum power value P_max = max_k(P[k]). Persistence mechanism: computed as D[k] = P_max - P[k] for each bin k, yielding a per-bin spectral decrease value; alternatively aggregated as a scalar S = (1/N) * Σ_k(P_max - P[k]) over all bins. Display trailer: spectral-decrease is a scalar or per-bin quantity expressed in the same units as the power spectrum. [formal: diminutio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-crossover is a spectral analysis parameter indicating the frequency within a defined sub-band at which the cumulative energy reaches 50% of the band's total energy — the band-local median frequency. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds, (2) the spectral energy values across frequency bins within the band. Computed by sorting frequency bins in ascending order by frequency, accumulating energy until the accumulated total reaches half the band's total energy; the frequency at that point is the crossover point. Distinct from spectral-band-centroid (weighted mean, sensitive to energy outliers) and spectral-band-rolloff (arbitrary threshold like 85%, indicating brightness); the crossover is the energy-median, robust to heavy-tailed distributions. Displayed as a scalar time series over analysis frames. [formal: centrum medium spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An analytic signal is a human-made complex-valued signal representation constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) by adding its Hilbert transform H{x(t)} as the imaginary component: z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}. This construction eliminates all negative-frequency components, resulting in a one-sided spectrum. The analytic signal carries three directly accessible parameters: (1) instantaneous amplitude (envelope) A(t) = |z(t)| = √(x(t)² + H{x(t)}²), (2) instantaneous phase φ(t) = arg(z(t)), and (3) instantaneous frequency f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ/dt. These parameters are computable in real time from a single observation, without ensemble averaging. The construction is used in communications (quadrature modulation/demodulation, SSB generation), audio analysis (phase vocoder phase unwrapping), geophysics, and biomedical signal processing. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic computation standard in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert) and embedded in communication system designs. [formal: signalis analyticus | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-asymmetry is a statistical descriptor quantifying how unevenly spectral energy is distributed across the frequency bins within a defined sub-band. Parameters: (1) lower and upper frequency bounds of the sub-band, (2) the energy values per frequency bin within the band. Computed as the normalized sum of absolute deviations from the band centroid: A = sum_i(|f_i - f_c| * E_i) / sum_i(E_i), where f_i is the frequency of bin i, f_c is the band centroid (weighted mean frequency), and E_i is the energy in bin i. The value is expressed in Hertz and indicates the spatial spread of energy around the centroid — higher values mean energy is concentrated toward one edge of the band, lower values mean energy is more centrally distributed. Persistence mechanism: arithmetic computation over the finite set of per-bin energy values for the given band and analysis frame. [formal: asymmetria spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral peak position is the frequency bin index (or frequency in Hz) of the maximum spectral energy magnitude within a spectrum or subband. Used to identify dominant resonant components. Parameters: search_range (full spectrum or subband), resolution (bin index or frequency). [formal: positio pinnaculi spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Instantaneous frequency is a human-made signal processing construct that measures the rate of change of the phase of a signal at each moment in time. It is defined as: f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ(t)/dt, where φ(t) = arg(z(t)) is the instantaneous phase of the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) and its Hilbert transform H{x(t)}. Unlike Fourier frequency (which represents a global property of the signal), instantaneous frequency is a local, time-varying quantity that tracks frequency modulation, chirp signals, and time-varying spectral content in real time. Parameters: (1) the phase unwrapping method applied to φ(t) (to avoid discontinuities at ±π), (2) the noise regularization method (to prevent divergence where amplitude is near zero). Persistence mechanism: standard in radar (chirp signal analysis), seismology, speech processing (formant tracking), and biomedical engineering (EEG/ECG frequency modulation analysis), implemented in DSP libraries and embedded in signal analysis instruments. [formal: frequency instantanea | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-peak-trough-ratio is a human-made spectral feature quantifying the contrast between dominant spectral peaks and the valleys between them within a defined frequency range. It is computed by first identifying local maxima (peaks) and minima (troughs) in the magnitude spectrum, then calculating the ratio of mean peak energy to mean trough energy: PTR = mean(E_peak) / mean(E_trough). Parameters: (1) a frequency range or band over which to compute the ratio, (2) a minimum peak height threshold to distinguish true peaks from noise, (3) a minimum distance between adjacent peaks. Values greater than 1 indicate a spectrum with prominent peaks above the trough floor; higher values indicate sharper, more tonal spectra. Persistence mechanism: computed numerically from discrete magnitude spectra, stored as a scalar value per analysis frame. [formal: ratio culminis et vallis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The spectral-band-concentration is a CONCEPT that quantifies how much of the total spectral power is concentrated in a subset of frequency bins. Parameters: a discrete spectral power distribution {P_i} over N bins, with total power P_total = ΣP_i. Computed as the ratio P_max/P_total where P_max is the maximum single-bin power, or equivalently via the Shannon entropy H = -Σp_i·log(p_i) of the normalized distribution p_i = P_i/P_total, with concentration = exp(-H) normalized to [0,1]. Persistence: the scalar value is maintained for a given spectral band as long as the underlying spectral representation is stable. [formal: latin | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Shimmer (amplitude perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the cycle-to-cycle variation of amplitude in a voiced speech signal. For a voiced segment segmented into N consecutive glottal cycles, each with amplitude A_i (peak or RMS of cycle i), the perturbation is the normalized cycle difference: APQ3 = (1/(3N)) * sum_i |A_{i+1} - A_i| / ( (1/N) * sum_i A_i ), or equivalently the standard deviation of the cycle amplitudes divided by their mean, reported in percent or in dB (20*log10(std/mean)). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle amplitude measure (peak or RMS), (3) the perturbation variant (APQ3 quotient or standard deviation). Small shimmer indicates amplitude stability (normal phonation); large shimmer indicates amplitude instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous amplitude tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. [formal: scintillatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Stress is the constructed phonological framework for analyzing prominence asymmetry within words and phrases: certain syllables are marked as stressed (more prominent) relative to their neighbors, and this marking is patterned by linguistic rule. Parameters: (1) degree - relative prominence against neighbors, primary and secondary; (2) realization - the cue bundle carrying stress: increased loudness, increased duration, and, in English, pitch height on the stressed syllable; (3) position - placement within the word, rule-governed in many languages and capable of distinguishing word identity (English 'record' noun vs verb); (4) phrase level - the organization of stresses into rhythmic groups in connected speech. Persistence: stress is realized in every utterance, transcribed in phonology, taught in phonetics and language pedagogy, and codified in dictionaries; it persists as a stable parameter of the linguistic system, changing only slowly across generations. [formal: stressum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The Hilbert transform is a linear operator that shifts the phase of every frequency component of a real-valued signal by 90 degrees (π/2 radians). Mathematically, for a signal x(t), the Hilbert transform is: H{x(t)} = (1/π) PV ∫₋∞^∞ x(τ)/(t−τ) dτ, where PV denotes the Cauchy principal value. In the frequency domain, it acts as an all-pass filter with frequency response H(f) = −j·sgn(f), multiplying positive frequencies by −j and negative frequencies by +j. The transform produces the quadrature component of x(t); combining x(t) with its Hilbert transform yields the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, from which instantaneous amplitude (envelope), instantaneous phase, and instantaneous frequency can be derived. Parameters: (1) the input signal domain (continuous-time or discrete via DFT-based implementation), (2) handling of the zero-frequency component (typically set to 0). Persistence mechanism: implemented in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert), used in communications (SSB modulation/demodulation), geophysics, and vibration analysis. [formal: transform Hilbert | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-kurtosis is a spectral analysis parameter measuring the fourth standardized moment of spectral energy distribution within a defined frequency sub-band. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds, (2) the spectral energy values across frequency bins within the band, (3) the mean and standard deviation of the band's energy distribution. Computed as E[(E - μ)⁴] / σ⁴ where E is spectral energy, μ is the band-mean energy, and σ is the band-standard deviation. High kurtosis indicates a distribution with heavy tails or a sharp peak — energy concentrated in few bins — while low kurtosis indicates a flatter, more uniform energy distribution across the band. Displayed as a scalar time series over analysis frames. [formal: kurtosis spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A gammatone-filter is a human-made linear time-invariant filter whose impulse response is an exponentially-modulated sinusoid — a gamma-shaped envelope h(t)=t^n·e^(−αt)·cos(2πf_c·t + φ) for t≥0 — that models the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery. It is typically realized as a cascade of four second-order resonator (complex-pole) sections, each tuned to a center frequency f_c, where the decay rate α and the resonance Q set the bandwidth (commonly mapped to the equivalent rectangular bandwidth, ERB). Parameters: (1) center frequency f_c; (2) bandwidth/selectivity (ERB or Q), which sets the decay rate α and the resonator pole placement; (3) the envelope order n and the modulation phase φ; (4) the number of cascade sections (classically four). Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard mathematical model — the closed-form impulse response plus the resonator-section difference equations — carried in auditory-modeling and audio-analysis literature (the classic gammatone and gammatone-filter-bank toolkits in MATLAB/Python, e.g. the Cochlea and gammatone libraries) and reused as a transform in cochlear and speech-processing front-ends. Boundary: it is a dynamic, time-domain resonator whose output is a decaying oscillation, not the static triangular mel-filter-bank that multiplies a power spectrum by fixed mel-spaced weights. [formal: resonantia gamma-soni | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-centroid is a spectral analysis parameter representing the center of mass of spectral energy distribution within a defined frequency sub-band. Spectral-evenness is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying how uniformly energy is distributed across the frequency bins of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band: the coefficient of variation of the per-bin energies. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |A_i|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. Computed as evenness = sigma/mu, where mu = (1/N) SUM E_i is the arithmetic mean of the per-bin energies and sigma = sqrt((1/N) SUM (E_i - mu)^2) is their standard deviation. The value is a dimensionless ratio: 0 when every bin carries identical energy (a perfectly flat spectrum), increasing without upper bound as energy concentrates in fewer bins. Being a ratio of two homogeneous quantities, it is level-invariant: scaling all bin energies by a constant leaves it unchanged. It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-evenness, which computes the same ratio over bins within [f_low, f_high). It differs from spectral-entropy (Shannon information content of the normalized energy distribution, bounded, logarithmic scale) and from spectral-flatness (geometric-mean-to-arithmetic-mean ratio, measuring flatness on a multiplicative scale): evenness is the dispersion of energies normalized by the arithmetic mean on an additive scale. Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of full-spectrum energy uniformity in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits and MIR feature pipelines. Effective bandwidth is a scalar width descriptor of a signal's spectral (or line) energy distribution, defined as the width of the ideal rectangular pulse having the same peak height and the same total energy as the distribution. Persistence mechanism: the cepstrum is computed as a deterministic mathematical transform, implemented in speech analysis and audio processing software, and used as an intermediate representation in cepstral feature extraction pipelines. Open quotient (OQ) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the fraction of the fundamental period during which the glottis is open in voiced phonation. From the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) (glottogram) and the fundamental period T0, the open phase is the interval between the flow maximum (Fmax) and the flow minimum (Fmin) — or between the zero crossings of the flow derivative — and OQ = open phase / T0. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites) from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. Electroglottography (EGG) is a non-invasive technique that measures glottal vocal-fold contact over time by passing a small alternating current through the vocal folds and recording the voltage across them. Because the glottal contact area modulates the electrical impedance of the vocal folds — high impedance when the glottis is open (air gap), low impedance when the folds are in contact — the peak-to-peak amplitude of the voltage is inversely related to glottal contact area, and its demodulated envelope, the electroglottogram (EGG waveform), tracks the open/close cycle of the glottis. Parameters: (1) excitation current — a small AC current kept below the safety threshold (typically ~0.5 mA peak at ~2.5 kHz); (2) electrode placement — two submental/neck electrodes completing the current path through the larynx; (3) demodulation — per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage measurement producing a continuous signal; (4) output — the electroglottogram, a time series whose amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area. Persistence mechanism: standardized EGG transducers and laryngeal analysis systems (Kay PENTAGRAM, the laryngograph), documented in clinical laryngology and voice-disorder assessment; the waveform persists as a measured time series of glottal contact. [formal: electroglottographia | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A crest-factor is a human-made audio engineering metric that quantifies the ratio of peak amplitude to RMS amplitude of a signal. Parameters: (1) A_peak = max|A(t)| the peak amplitude, (2) A_rms = √(1/T ∫₀ᵀ A(t)² dt) the RMS amplitude over window T. The persistence mechanism is the scalar ratio: CF = A_peak / A_rms. An equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth (ERB) is a human-made, frequency-dependent unit of filter bandwidth used to describe the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery. It is defined as the width of a rectangular (flat) bandpass filter that would pass the same energy as a given auditory filter centered at frequency f. The standard empirical expression is ERB(f) = 24.7·(4.37·f + 1), with f in kHz and the result in Hz, so the equivalent width is about 104 Hz near 0.1 kHz and grows toward roughly 100·f at high frequencies — the auditory filter narrows relative to its center as f rises. Parameters: (1) the center frequency f (kHz); (2) the chosen fitting curve — the Glasberg & Moore (1990) expression is canonical, with alternative fits in the literature. Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard psychophysically derived formula carried in the audiology and auditory-modeling literature (Glasberg & Moore 1990; Moore's auditory-filter and loudness work) and applied operationally to set the spacing and bandwidth of gammatone, bark, and auditory-filter-bank filters. Boundary: it is a unit of measure — a single number in Hz attached to a center frequency — not the auditory filter itself, not a signal's spectral bandwidth, and distinct from the generic signal-processing 'bandwidth' entry. [formal: latitudo rectanguli aequivalens | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-spread is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy across the frequency bins within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum at a given analysis frame. It is the square root of the band's second central moment: the energy-weighted standard deviation of bin frequencies about the band's centroid. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high), (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |X[k]|^2 for bins whose center frequencies fall within [f_low, f_high), (3) the analysis frame window. Computed as spread = sqrt( sum E_i * (f_i - c)^2 / sum E_i ), where c = sum(f_i * E_i) / sum(E_i) is the spectral-band-centroid of the same band. The value is in hertz: a large spread means energy is dispersed across the band, a small spread means energy is concentrated near the centroid. Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of band dispersion in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits (e.g. librosa's spectral_spread) and MIR feature pipelines. [formal: dispersio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-variance quantifies the dispersion of power values across frequency bins. Given a power spectrum P[k] for k = 0..N-1, the spectral mean μ = (1/N)ΣP[k] and the spectral variance σ² = (1/N)Σ(P[k] - μ)². Parameters: (1) the power spectrum P[k] as the input domain, (2) the normalization scheme (mean or total-power normalization). The persistence mechanism is the second central moment of P[k] over the frequency index, which distinguishes narrowband spectra (low variance) from broadband spectra (high variance). The root-mean-square amplitude of a power spectrum, computed as the square root of the mean of squared spectral amplitude values across frequency bins. The spectral-band-evenness is a CONCEPT that quantifies how uniformly spectral energy is distributed across a frequency band. Computed by sorting spectral magnitudes in descending order, accumulating their squared values, and finding the frequency at which the cumulative sum reaches rolloff_percent times the total spectral energy. For a frequency band with N energy bins having energies E_1, E_2, ..., E_N within frequencies f_1, f_2, ..., f_N: the effective bandwidth is the ratio of the sum of energies to the maximum energy, scaled by the per-bin frequency spacing delta_f. Spectral tenuity is a metric quantifying how thin or filamentary the spectral energy distribution is across frequency bins. Unlike sparseness which measures concentration count, tenuity measures the ratio of peak energy to total energy, capturing how narrowly energy clusters around dominant components. Computed as peak magnitude divided by mean magnitude across active bins. [formal: tenuitas spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-roll-off is a frequency value in Hz that marks the point below which a specified cumulative fraction (default 0.85) of the total spectral energy is contained. Parameters: (1) a power spectrum P[k] for k = 0, ..., N-1 with associated frequency bins f[k], (2) a cumulative threshold τ ∈ [0,1] (default 0.85). Computation: sort P[k] by f[k], compute cumulative sum C[k] = Σ_{i=0}^{k} P[i], then find the smallest k* such that C[k*]/Σ_{i=0}^{N-1} P[i] ≥ τ; roll-off = f[k*]. Display: roll-off(τ) = f[k*] where C[k*]/E_total ≥ τ and C[k*-1]/E_total < τ [formal: mind | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The time required for an amplitude envelope to fall from its peak level to a specified lower level after the attack phase. Spectral-band-band-center is a spectral analysis parameter representing the geometric mean center frequency of spectral energy within a defined frequency sub-band. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds, (2) the spectral energy values across frequency bins within the band. Computed as the geometric mean: exp(sum(f_i * ln(E_i)) / sum(E_i)) where f_i is the frequency of bin i and E_i is the spectral energy at that bin — distinct from spectral-band-centroid's arithmetic weighted mean. Values approach the geometric center of the energy distribution, which is lower than the arithmetic centroid when the distribution is right-skewed. Persistence mechanism: arithmetic computation over per-bin energy values for a given band and analysis frame, displayed as a scalar time series. Spectral-flow is the temporal evolution of spectral energy distribution across consecutive analysis frames, capturing how energy moves between frequency bands over time. Spectral-distribution is the ordered per-bin energy vector of a full spectrum: for a spectral decomposition with N frequency bins indexed i=1..N, each with center frequency f_i and complex amplitude A_i, the distribution is the ordered vector v = (|A_1|², |A_2|², ..., |A_N|²) covering all bins of the full spectrum, unbounded by any sub-band. A critical-band is a human-made psychoacoustic construct representing the frequency resolution unit of the human auditory system — the effective bandwidth of auditory filters at a given center frequency. It quantifies how the ear's basilar membrane separates frequencies into perceptually independent channels. At any center frequency f, the critical-band width approximates the ERB(f) = 24.7·(4.37·f+1) Hz (f in kHz), which is the width of a rectangular bandpass filter passing the same energy as the auditory filter at that frequency. Parameters: (1) center frequency f; (2) the bandwidth rule (ERB approximation). Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard psychoacoustic concept codified in Zwicker's work (Zwicker 1961, 'Schnell und zeitliche Abhängigkeit der Lautheit'), ITU-R BS.516, ISO 532, and carried in audio analysis, sound design, and psychoacoustic modeling literature. Boundary: it is a model of perceptual frequency resolution, not the physical basilar membrane itself, not the gammatone filter realization, and not the bark-scale (which maps frequencies onto critical-band numbers). [formal: banda critica | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral sparseness is a metric quantifying how concentrated spectral energy is across frequency bins. High sparseness indicates energy concentrated in few bins (e.g. tonal signals); low sparseness indicates diffuse energy (e.g. noise). Computed as (sum of magnitudes)^2 divided by (number_of_bins times sum of squared magnitudes). [formal: sparsitas spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An auditory-filter is a human-made linear bandpass filter whose center frequency and bandwidth are chosen to match the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery at that frequency, so that it approximates the response of a single cochlear channel. The standard parameterization sets the bandwidth to the equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth ERB(f)=24.7·(4.37·f+1) at center f (kHz), with the filter shape given by a gamma-shaped (exponentially-modulated sinusoid) or Lorentzian (ROEX) impulse response. Parameters: (1) center frequency f; (2) the selectivity/bandwidth rule (ERB, or a constant-Q Lorentzian); (3) the impulse-response shape — the gamma (gammatone) form or the rectangular-excitation (ROEX/Lorentzian) form; (4) the cascade order when realized as resonator sections. Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard model of single-channel cochlear selectivity in the auditory-periphery literature (the gammatone and ROEX families; Moore's and Glasberg & Moore's auditory-filter work) and is the element from which filter banks are built. Boundary: it is a single analysis filter, not the array (filter-bank / mel-filterbank) that places many in parallel, and not the gammatone-filter alone — the gammatone-filter is the canonical resonator realization of this construct, so the two are distinct kinds, not the same thing. [formal: filtrum auditivum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-spread is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy across the frequency bins of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N with center frequencies f_i, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |X[k_i]|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. The value is in hertz: a large spread means energy is dispersed across the spectrum, a small spread means energy is concentrated near the centroid. It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-spread, which restricts the same formula to bins within [f_low, f_high). Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of full-spectrum dispersion in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits and MIR feature pipelines. [formal: dispersio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

[formal: latin | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A bark-spectrogram is a two-dimensional time-frequency matrix where rows are bark-scale frequency bins and columns are temporal frames. Parameters: (1) N bark-scale bins indexed 0..N-1, (2) frame hop size h in samples, (3) window function w applied per frame. Computation: for each frame f, apply FFT to windowed segment, convert linear-frequency indices to bark scale via Bark(f) = 13*arctan(0.00076*f) + 3.5*arctan((f/7500)^2), accumulate energy into bark bins, normalize by bin bandwidth. Persistence: the matrix values are the squared magnitudes accumulated per bark bin, stored as a sequence of N×T matrices. Display: a heatmap with time on the x-axis, Bark units on the y-axis, color representing log-energy.

Inverse-filtering is a signal processing technique that estimates and removes the effect of a known or estimated system transfer function from a signal, effectively recovering the original input that passed through that system. The method operates by: (1) obtaining the estimated transfer function H(z) of the system to be inverted (e.g., the linear-prediction filter for the vocal tract), (2) constructing the inverse filter H_inv(z) = 1/H(z), (3) filtering the observed signal with H_inv(z) to produce the residual or excitation signal. Parameters: (1) the transfer function to invert — typically a finite-order all-pole model estimated from the signal itself, (2) the input signal — the observed output of the system, (3) the inversion method — direct division in the z-domain, iterative regularization, or frequency-domain division. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation: the inverse filter is encoded in DSP software (e.g., Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documented in signal processing textbooks, and standardized in speech analysis toolkits for source-filter separation. Linguistic register is the map of the system of situationally differentiated language varieties a speech community develops and maintains — the varieties a community deploys for different communicative situations (colloquial, formal, technical, ceremonial, professional) — carved along three parameters. (1) The situational axis: the dimensions along which the varieties are organized are field (the subject matter and activity in which the language is deployed), tenor (the social relations and roles between participants), and mode (the channel and the participatory structure of the discourse); a variety is a conventionalized set of lexical, grammatical, and prosodic choices indexed to the situation, so that the same speaker deploys different varieties in different situations. (2) The boundary lines that separate the map from its neighbours: register is indexed to situation, which distinguishes it from dialect (indexed to region and social group) and from genre (a type of discourse text rather than a variety of the language itself); and it is distinct from the institutional register — an official list maintained by an authority with legal or institutional force — in that a linguistic register is updated by the speech community's convention, not by institutional mandate, and no authority stands behind its entries. (3) The map, not the territory: the entry names the systematic description the community and the discipline build over the natural variation of speech — the inventory of varieties and the dimensions that organize it — not the natural variation itself. Persistence: the varieties persist as social convention — acquired in socialization, maintained through institutional reinforcement (courts, academies, professions, liturgy), and relearned by each generation; the map persists as the stable sub-field of linguistics called register analysis, its dimensions codified in textbooks and corpora. [formal: regiter linguae | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

Neurolinguistics persists as an active research enterprise that generates testable hypotheses about how the brain implements language, uses these hypotheses to interpret clinical conditions (aphasia, dyslexia, speech disorders), and informs brain-computer interfaces for language restoration. Paradigmatic methods: fMRI and EEG mapping of language tasks, lesion-symptom mapping in aphasia patients, intracranial electrophysiology, and computational modeling of neural language processing. [formal: neurolinguistica | substrate: brain | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral-smoothness is a spectral analysis measure that quantifies how smoothly the per-bin energy values change across frequency in a full spectrum. Parameters: (1) the spectral estimate (periodogram, Welch's method, or spectrogram slice), (2) the per-bin energy vector across all frequency bins. Computed as smoothness = 1 - (1/N) * Σ|E[i+1] - E[i]| / mean(E) where E[i] is the energy of bin i, N is the number of bins, and mean(E) is the arithmetic mean of all bin energies. Values range from 0 (highly irregular spectrum with abrupt energy changes) to approaching 1 (very smooth spectrum with gradual energy transitions). Displayed as a scalar time series over analysis frames. [formal: planities spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.30]

Persistence: intonation is realized in every produced utterance, analyzed in intonation notation (e.g., ToBI), taught in language pedagogy, and studied in phonology; it persists as long as speech carries meaning through pitch. [formal: intonatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cognitive-linguistics is a human-made approach to linguistics — the study of language as a manifestation of general cognitive abilities, including categorization, conceptualization, metaphorical reasoning, and embodied experience. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory framework denies that language operates as an autonomous module separate from general cognition; language structure reflects domain-general cognitive mechanisms like attention, memory, pattern recognition, and conceptual blending; (2) the empirical evidence comes from cross-linguistic analysis of how semantic structure, syntactic patterns, and figurative language systematically reflect cognitive universals (spatial reasoning, embodiment, force-dynamics) rather than language-internal formal rules. Cognitive-linguistics persists as a theoretical framework that produces models of construction grammar, conceptual metaphor theory, and cognitive semantics, generating testable predictions about language use, acquisition, and processing that compete with modularist accounts. Cepstral-mean-variance normalization (CMVN) is a signal processing technique that normalizes cepstral coefficient vectors by computing the mean and variance across an utterance (or a sliding window) and applying z-score normalization to each frame. Derivation is a human-made morphological operation — the process by which a language creates a new lexeme from an existing one by adding derivational material. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) lexeme change: the output is a new lexeme with a distinct dictionary identity from the input (happy → happiness is one lexeme becoming another; walk → walked is NOT derivation, because walked is an inflected form of the same lexeme as walk). This lexeme-change criterion is the decisive boundary from inflection. (2) derivational material: the operation is carried by a bound morpheme (affix) or, in some languages, by a change of stress, vowel, or other internal modification that contributes derivational meaning (English sing → song: an ablaut-derived noun; by contrast the tense forms sang and sung remain inflected forms of the same lexeme as sing). (3) conventionalized meaning: the derivational material contributes a systematic, predictable meaning (-ness 'state of being', un- 'negation', -er 'agent') that transforms the input lexeme's meaning in a rule-governed way. Paradigmatic cases: happy + -ness → happiness (new lexeme); write → writer (new lexeme, agentive). Derivation persists as a productive rule — speakers coin new derived lexemes on the fly — and as a stable category of grammatical description: derivational affixes are catalogued in the morphological inventory of each language. [formal: derivatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
